anatomy.lede: A long black fish with two kinds of headlight, an eye tuned to red, and a jaw that swings open like a trapdoor.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its retina holds two visual pigments most sensitive at about 520 and 540 nm, plus a chlorophyll-derived pigment that boosts its sensitivity to red.

hotspots.label: Far-red light organ
hotspots.text: The light organ below the eye shines far-red, peaking above 700 nm. Far-red light organs like this may have evolved up to three times among the loosejaw dragonfishes.

hotspots.label: Postorbital light organ
hotspots.text: A smaller light organ behind the eye gives off blue light, like those of most deep-sea animals.

hotspots.label: Head joint
hotspots.text: Where the skull meets the spine, only a flexible notochord remains. It lets the head tip far up and back, opening the mouth to a gape of up to 120 degrees.

hotspots.label: Lower jaw
hotspots.text: Its jaws are long and its prey relatively large. Compared with its southern look-alike, Malacosteus australis, its jaws are somewhat larger.

stats.label: Peak wavelength of its red light

senses.lede: In a sea where almost every eye sees only blue, the loosejaw can see the red light it makes.

senses.name: A borrowed red boost
senses.text: It lacks the most red-sensitive visual pigments found in its relatives, and instead uses a mixture of altered bacteriochlorophyll c and d to extend its sensitivity into the red.

senses.name: A single opsin gene
senses.text: Molecular analysis found only one opsin gene in its genome, forming a pigment pair with two slightly different versions of the light-catching chromophore.

senses.name: Bigger eyes in males
senses.text: Males have larger eye lenses than females. A model suggests this lets them spot the light organs of the opposite sex from farther away.

body.lede: The loosejaw's head is built for two jobs: making unusual light and swallowing big prey.

systems.title: A true head joint
systems.text: In most bony fishes the shoulder girdle is braced against the skull. In loosejaws it is not, and a folded sheath of notochord forms a working joint between skull and spine.

systems.title: Lights wired to different nerves
systems.text: The far-red organ of Malacosteus is supplied by a different branch of the trigeminal nerve than the similar organs of related genera, evidence that red light evolved separately in each.

genome.lede: No nuclear genome has been published, but its mitochondrial genome is one of the odder ones known in fishes.

findings.title: A large, complex mitogenome
findings.text: Its mitochondrial genome is 21,263 base pairs long, with two copies of a 1,198 bp inverted repeat and a long run of short repeated elements.

mind.lede: No one has watched a stoplight loosejaw hunt or court, so its behaviour is inferred from its body.

studies.title: A private waveband
studies.text: Because other deep-sea animals are blind to far-red light, loosejaws may use it to light up prey and signal to their own kind unseen.

studies.title: Closing the detection gap
studies.text: Males have larger postorbital light organs, so females should see males first. Larger eyes in males may even out the distance at which each sex can find the other.

survival.lede: Living below the reach of sunlight, the loosejaw hunts with a light its prey cannot see.

tactics.title: An invisible searchlight
tactics.text: Red light does not penetrate deep water, so most deep-sea prey cannot see it, and the fish can light up its prey unseen.

tactics.title: Staying deep
tactics.text: It has been suggested that, unlike many deep-sea fishes, it does not migrate up towards the surface at night and stays below 500 m.
